title: If God Compels You to This Fate...
text:
If God compels you to this fate:

To die alone, with no one beside your bed

to hear your last word in sorrow

and mark your wavering pulse with tears;

then pray in solitude: Oh Lord, come tenderly!

By your son forgotten in the vineyard of red misery,

by the wild life that stirs in the world,

by the abandoned garden where agony

fell like a bloody tide from your brow,

by all this desolation, comfort me.

There are no friends or laments beside me,

no angel rises between my face and yours,

but I ask you: pause and pluck the rose of my life;

smile, changing this mortal sorrow into divine eternity.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the solitary deathbed prayer and its plea for mortal pain to become eternity.

title: That the Whole Face of the World Has Changed, I Would Say
text:
That the whole face of the world has changed, I would say,

since I heard the steps of your soul move

lightly, oh, very lightly!, beside me, slipping

between me and that terrible edge of death,


so clear, where I thought I would sink; but I was lifted

up to love and could know a new rhythm

to rock life. The cup of bitterness

that God gives us at birth, I will gladly drain,


praising its sweetness, my love, beside you.

The name of lands and the name of sky are altered

according to where you are or may someday be.


And this lute and song of mine, which I once loved

(the singing angels know it well), I love them

only because your name mingles in what they say.
editorial_note: This Spanish variant keeps the altered-world sonnet in a more sentence-driven form.

title: I Give Thanks to All
text:
I give thanks to all who have loved me in their hearts,

with the thanks and love that are in mine. Deep thanks to all

who have lingered at the walls of this prison

to hear my music in its most intense pain,

always floating onward, filling the space

of the pagan temple, beyond words.


You, who sink and fall into my voice

when grief carries you away, the divine instrument

of art unfolds at your feet

to hear what I have said through tears.

Teach me how to thank you. Teach me how

to see the meaning of my life in future years,

and to feel that love endures in the life that fades.
editorial_note: The translation keeps gratitude as a prison-wall music heard through pain and tears.

title: Say It, Say It Again
text:
Say it, say it again, and repeat once more

that you love me, though that repeated word,

on your lips, recalls the cuckoo's song.

And do not forget that fresh spring never


came to mountain or plain, to valley or woods,

in its whole greenness, without the cuckoo's voice.

It greets me in the shadows, my beloved, uncertain,

that voice of a spirit, and in my anguished doubt,


I cry: "Say again that you love me!" Who

fears an excess of stars, though they fill the heavens,

or an excess of flowers girdling the whole year?


Say that you love me, say that you love me: renew

the silver ringing; but think, my beloved,

of loving me also with the soul, in silence.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the repeated request for spoken love while preserving the final turn toward silent soul-love.

title: Land of Loneliness
text:
With time, bodies grow used

to walking completely

        alone

over the land of loneliness.

The vague sensations, the

        memories

of the places where we found

someone with

        whom to speak, someone who would listen

to our words as evening

        falls,

slowly fade away, like

tracks the wind

        extinguishes and disorders.

And the warm echo of the old encounter

does not

        persist in the voice, in the language

with which we learned to name

        things.

Only night remains. And we lose ourselves

in the long silence of

        empty

streets. And when dawn arrives

we feel cold and

        breathe death.

October 16,

        1975
editorial_note: The translation preserves the dated ending and the poem's slow erasure of shared language.
